content: Dysuria is characterized by pain, burning, stinging, or itching sensations in the urethra or urethral meatus that occur during or immediately after urination. This discomfort arises because the contraction of the bladder muscles and the peristaltic movement of the urethra bring urine into contact with inflamed mucosal surfaces. This interaction stimulates pain receptors, leading to the sensation of pain or burning. Dysuria can affect both males and females, but it is more commonly observed in females. This is primarily due to anatomical differences, as females have a shorter and straighter urethra compared to males, whose urethra is longer and curved. The shorter distance in females allows bacteria to reach the bladder more easily, increasing the risk of urinary tract infections (UTIs), which are a leading cause of dysuria. Additionally, improper wiping techniques in females, such as wiping from back to front instead of front to back, can introduce bacteria from the rectal area to the urethral opening, further predisposing them to infections and dysuria. The pathophysiology of dysuria varies depending on its underlying cause. In cases of inflammation, such as those caused by UTIs, the contraction of the bladder and urethral peristalsis brings urine into contact with inflamed mucosa, activating sensory nerves and pain receptors. This results in sensations of pain, burning, stinging, or itching. Inflammatory or neuropathic processes can heighten the sensitivity of these receptors, exacerbating symptoms. Dysuria can also result from inflammation in adjacent organs, such as the colon. Non-inflammatory causes, including urinary stones, tumors, trauma, or foreign bodies, can irritate the bladder or urethral mucosa, leading to similar symptoms. Dysuria can be classified into two broad categories: infectious and non-infectious. Infectious causes include UTIs, urethritis, kidney or prostate infections, vaginal infections, sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), and interstitial cystitis. Non-infectious causes encompass foreign bodies or stones in the urinary tract, trauma, benign prostatic hyperplasia, tumors, certain medications, anatomical abnormalities, and menopause. Certain life-threatening conditions, such as toxic epidermal necrolysis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, can also present with dysuria. More common causes include balanitis, cervicitis, lower urinary tract infections, pelvic inflammatory disease, pyelonephritis, urethritis, and vaginitis. Treatment for dysuria is determined by its underlying cause. For the most common cause, urinary tract infections, empiric antibiotic therapy is typically initiated. If dysuria is caused by renal stones, management depends on the size and location of the stones. Stones smaller than 5 mm often pass spontaneously, and patients are advised to stay hydrated and strain their urine to confirm stone passage. Larger stones, exceeding 5 mm, may require interventions such as extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), or, in some cases, open surgery. In males with chronic prostatitis, oral antibiotics are considered after obtaining a urine culture to guide therapy.
